Laish
LAY-ish
proper noun
Hebrew Layish, “a lion,” the old name of the northern city later called Dan.

📖 Biblical Definition

Laish was a city in the far north of the land, near the headwaters of the Jordan, inhabited by a careless people who dwelt “quiet and secure, after the manner of the Zidonians,” far from any that might trouble them (Judg 18:7). When the tribe of Dan, unable to possess its allotted coast, sent men to seek a place to dwell, the spies marked Laish as a fat and unguarded prize; and six hundred armed Danites went up, smote the people with the edge of the sword, and burnt the city with fire (Judg 18:27). They rebuilt it and called it Dan, after the name of their father (Judg 18:29); it is also named Leshem in the book of Joshua (Josh 19:47). But the conquest of Laish was no act of faith. The Danites carried with them the stolen graven image of Micah and the renegade Levite, and set up idolatry in the new city, which continued “all the time that the house of God was in Shiloh” (Judg 18:31). Thus Dan, the northernmost city of Israel, became from its founding a seat of false worship, and later one of Jeroboam’s two golden calves was placed there. Laish stands as a warning that men may gain a possession and yet defile it from the first stone with the worship of an idol.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The northern city, formerly Laish or Leshem, taken by the Danites and renamed Dan; a seat of idolatry from its founding.

expand to see more

LAISH, an ancient city near the source of the Jordan in the far north of Canaan.

Its people dwelt careless and secure after the manner of the Zidonians (Judg 18:7).

The Danites took it, burnt it, rebuilt it, and called it Dan (Judg 18:29).

It is also called Leshem in the inheritance of Dan (Josh 19:47).

There the Danites set up Micah’s graven image, defiling the city from the first (Judg 18:31).

📖 Key Scripture

Judg 18:7 — "Then the five men departed, and came to Laish, and saw the people that were therein, how they dwelt careless, after the manner of the Zidonians, quiet and secure; and there was no magistrate in the land, that might put them to shame in any thing;"

Judg 18:27 — "And they took the things which Micah had made, and the priest which he had, and came unto Laish, unto a people that were at quiet and secure: and they smote them with the edge of the sword, and burnt the city with fire."

Judg 18:29 — "And they called the name of the city Dan, after the name of Dan their father, who was born unto Israel: howbeit the name of the city was Laish at the first."

Josh 19:47 — "And the coast of the children of Dan went out too little for them: therefore the children of Dan went up to fight against Leshem, and took it, and smote it with the edge of the sword, and possessed it, and dwelt therein, and called Leshem, Dan, after the name of Dan their father."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A place-name, not a contested doctrine; its lesson is that a possession seized for self and defiled with idolatry is cursed from the first.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Danites’ conquest of Laish was not obedience but self-will: they sought ease and a fat land, took it by force apart from God’s leading, and brought a stolen idol with them. A people may prosper outwardly and yet build their house upon false worship; such a foundation is rotten however fair the city.

Laish, renamed Dan, became a fountain of idolatry for all Israel, for there Jeroboam set one of his golden calves. The lesson is that sin planted at the founding of a thing spreads through its whole history. What the Danites carried up to Laish poisoned the worship of the nation for centuries; small compromise at the beginning becomes great corruption in the end.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The name means “a lion,” one of several Hebrew words for that beast, here fixed to the old city of Dan.

expand to see more

Laish — Hebrew Layish, “a lion.”

The same word is used for the strong lion in Job and Isaiah.

The city was also called Leshem, a variant of the name.

After its capture it bore forever the name of Dan.

The lion-city became a den of idols in the north of Israel.

Usage

"Like the Danites at Laish, men may win an easy prize and ruin it with idolatry from the first day."

"Laish teaches that quiet and security without God are no true safety, for the careless city fell in a day."

"What was carried up to Laish defiled a nation, proving that small compromise breeds great corruption."
